name: FamilyWall Premium
subcategory: family organization, recipes and household inventory
tagline: Share family calendar, lists, messages, and selected location check-ins

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Shared calendar, shopping lists, to-do lists, messenger and contact book; no numeric family-member cap disclosed.
tiers.notes: Most features free, but premium gates several advanced features.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Family subscription; Google/Outlook sync, meal planner, budget tracker, timetable, real-time location, place alerts, 25 GB storage, audio/video messages.

pricing.freeTierCaps: $0; shared calendar, shopping lists, to-do lists, messenger and contact book; no numeric family-member cap disclosed.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; 30-day trial; auto-renews unless canceled at least 24 hours before period end
pricing.hiddenCosts: Premium Plan features are applied to the first 5 circles; unused free-trial portion may be forfeited if purchasing during trial; location sharing can increase device battery use.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For FamilyWall Premium, share family calendar, lists, messages, and selected location check-ins. The hard boundary is mobile apps, sync, location services, messaging, storage, and family adoption, plus sync, integrations, and household adoption.
coreLoopDIY: Share a family calendar, lists, messages, and selected location check-ins, print or share a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
whatYouLose: mobile apps, sync, location services, messaging, storage, and family adoption
ongoingBurden: multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for FamilyWall Premium because household apps survive when every family member actually uses them and the data stays current across devices. The recurring cost buys multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Mealie
priorArt.desc: Active open-source recipe manager and meal planner for households.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Family Tools Basic
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Calendar, chores, and lists are free; family messaging and location check-ins are missing.

rejectedAlternatives.name: FamilyWall Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Calendar, lists, and chat are free; locating family members is a Premium feature.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Homechart
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Calendar and household tools look right; sharing a household is paid, before location even enters the room.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium plan and a single-household organizer DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for FamilyWall Premium in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and a local-first PWA; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: share a family calendar, lists, messages, and selected location check-ins, print or share a simple plan, and keep the data portable and owner-controlled.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create household members, shared lists, calendar items, recipes or inventory records, and assignments.
Provide fast mobile-first capture with large controls, offline queueing, and conflict-safe sync to one server.
Support recurring chores or events, reminders, completion history, and printable views.
Add CSV or JSON import and export plus photo attachments with clear size limits.
Allow private and shared items and make every change attributable and undoable.
Add backups, household export, member removal, and a simple invite code.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out retailer ordering and proprietary product catalogs.
Deliberately leave out broad smart-home integrations.
Deliberately leave out large public recipe libraries and polished native mobile clients.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
